paragraphs.en: Anyone who has sat in a traffic jam knows that big cities have a transport problem. As urban populations grow and more families buy cars, roads that once seemed wide enough become crowded for much of the day. The result is not only lost time but also noise, air pollution and stress. City authorities around the world are therefore looking for ways to move more people while putting fewer vehicles on the streets.

For many large cities, the backbone of the solution is an underground railway. A metro can carry enormous numbers of passengers quickly, and because it runs beneath the streets, it is not affected by the traffic above. The drawback is cost: building tunnels and stations is extremely expensive and can take many years, which is why new lines are often planned decades in advance.

Buses are cheaper and more flexible, since routes can be changed without major construction. However, a bus stuck in traffic is no faster than a car. To deal with this, some cities have introduced dedicated bus lanes, and a few have built rapid bus systems in which buses run on separate roads and passengers pay before boarding, so that the service works rather like a metro above ground.

Cycling is also receiving more attention. In several European cities, a large share of daily journeys is made by bicycle, largely because safe, separated cycle paths have been built over many years. Planners have learned that painting a line on a busy road is not enough: people will only cycle in large numbers if they feel protected from cars. Bike-sharing schemes, which allow users to rent a bicycle for a short trip, have spread to many countries.

A more controversial approach is to make driving itself more expensive. A number of cities, including London, Stockholm and Singapore, charge drivers a fee for entering busy central areas or using the most crowded roads at certain times. Supporters point out that such congestion charges reduce traffic and raise money that can be spent on public transport. Critics argue that they are unfair to people on low incomes who have no real alternative to driving.

Tashkent offers an interesting example of a city adapting to rapid growth. Its metro, which opened in 1977, was the first in Central Asia, and its stations are famous for their richly decorated halls. In recent years the network has been expanded considerably, including a new line that runs above ground around parts of the city, and many old buses have been replaced with newer ones. As in other growing cities, the challenge is to make public transport attractive enough that residents choose it over their cars.
